analysis.one_liner: Lifts the Jones Act requirement that cargo to Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico sail on U.S. ships.
analysis.headline: A bill to let cheaper foreign-flag ships carry cargo to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico died in committee with no cosponsors and never reached a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jones Act requires cargo moving between U.S. ports to travel on ships built, owned, and crewed in the United States, which makes shipping to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico far more expensive. This bill would have exempted that noncontiguous trade, letting lower-cost foreign vessels carry the freight — while still requiring them to employ U.S. citizen crew, meet international labor and environmental rules, and be sued in U.S. courts for crew injuries. The bill was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other island territories, who currently pay some of the highest shipping costs in the country because the Jones Act bars cheaper foreign-flag vessels. Retail goods, food, fuel, and cars could arrive more cheaply. Foreign-flag shipping companies would also gain access to a market now closed to them, and U.S. seamen would get a guaranteed home-state court for injury lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico

how_it_helps.text: Exempts cargo shipped between the 48 contiguous states and Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the territories from the Jones Act, so foreign vessels carrying this freight no longer have to charge the premium rates of a closed U.S.-only market.
Requires foreign vessels entering this trade to employ U.S. citizens to the same extent required of U.S.-registered vessels, so some American seafaring jobs would remain.

Makes every vessel in U.S. coastwise trade — foreign or American — follow minimum international labor standards and all U.S. and international environmental rules, with consistent standards applied so foreign ships are not held to a lower bar than U.S. ones.

Lets a seaman injured or killed working for a foreign employer without a U.S. office sue in the U.S. district court nearest where the injury happened, instead of being forced to chase the employer into a distant or foreign forum.
Keeps some shipboard liability coverage available by letting an employer enroll crew in Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act plans.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag Jones Act carriers — the shipping lines whose freight rates are protected by the closed domestic market — would face new competition and lose revenue. U.S. shipyards, which depend on Jones Act vessels being built domestically (the bill only admits foreign-built ships), would lose that guaranteed demand. Some U.S. merchant mariner jobs and wages, and the fleet Congress keeps for national-security sealift, would shrink.

drawbacks.text: Opening noncontiguous trade would cut revenue for U.S.-flag carriers and orders for U.S. shipyards, and the bill admits only foreign-built vessels into the new trade, so American shipbuilding demand would drop.

The labor section lets an employer elect Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation coverage for crew, and that election becomes the 'exclusive' remedy — meaning injured seafarers covered by it could no longer sue for full damages, a tradeoff a seafarer's advocate would question.

A smaller U.S.-flag fleet weakens the merchant marine that federal law has long maintained as a national-defense sealift reserve, which is why the bill was also referred to the Armed Services Committee.

Enforcement of the bill's labor and environmental standards on foreign vessels depends on the Transportation Secretary's determinations, and the bill sets civil penalties of only up to $10,000 per violation for unlawful transfer of vessels in the new trade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico the benefit is direct and large: island shipping costs under the Jones Act are a well-documented driver of their cost of living, and this bill targets exactly that trade while adding labor, environmental, and court-access protections. The real costs fall on U.S.-flag carriers, shipyards, and merchant mariners — a concentrated group — and on a national-defense fleet that shrinks with each lost Jones Act route. The bill's protections for crew are uneven: the same section that guarantees a local court also lets employers swap a seaman's right to sue for a workers' compensation schedule. On balance it is a genuine consumer bargain with real but narrower costs, and it received no apparent help toward enactment: zero cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and a subcommittee until the 108th Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case of Hawaii introduced the bill on July 24, 2003; the House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and also to Armed Services.
The next day, the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee sent it to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, where it stayed.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the bill's action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag Jones Act shipping lines and the shipyards that build their vessels are better off: the closed domestic market that protects their rates stayed intact, and island consumers kept paying the higher shipping costs embedded in their prices.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or vote

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never acted on it

against.name: Jones Act shipping industry
against.role: U.S.-flag carriers protected by the coastwise law
against.what_they_did: Long opposed every attempt to open noncontiguous shipping to foreign vessels, which would end the premium rates the law secures for them

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the bill is unknown beyond a single Democratic sponsor from an affected island state.

industries.note: The Jones Act guarantees these carriers a closed market for cargo between U.S. ports, and rates to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico are among the highest in domestic freight. The bill would have let cheaper foreign vessels into that trade, cutting their protected revenue.

Jones Act carriers must buy American-built ships, which is a guaranteed order book for U.S. yards. The bill only admits vessels not built in the United States, so the shipyards' captive demand in this trade would disappear.

International carriers would win access to the noncontiguous trade for the first time since 1920. Their gain would come from competing on price, which is exactly what island consumers would benefit from.

industries.industry: U.S. merchant mariners and maritime unions
industries.note: More vessels in the trade would have to employ U.S. citizens and follow international labor standards, but cheaper foreign competition would shrink the U.S.-flag fleet and the mariner jobs tied to it. The bill's compensation election could also cap some crew members' recovery after injury.
